title: Backup, Recovery, and Security
description: Protect your data with backups and recovery models, and control access using authentication, authorization, roles, and GRANT/REVOKE/DENY.

data.text: The final pillar of database administration is protecting your data: making sure you can recover from hardware failure or user error, and controlling who can see and change what. This lesson covers both.
SQL Server offers three main backup types that form a layered protection strategy. You typically use all three together.

rows: Entire database at a point in time
All changes since the last full backup
After the full, before log backups
All transactions since the last log backup

data.title: Full backup
data.code:
BACKUP DATABASE HR
TO   DISK = 'D:\backup\hr.bak'
WITH INIT,
     NAME = 'HR-Full Database Backup';

data.title: The D:\ path
data.text: The backup folder must already exist — BACKUP DATABASE will not create it for you. In production, use a dedicated backup drive or network share, never the same disk as your data files.
A recovery model controls how much transaction log is retained and what restore options you have. It is a database-level setting:

rows: No — only to last full/diff backup
Yes (but not for point-in-time during bulk ops)

data.title: Set recovery model to FULL
data.code:
ALTER DATABASE HR
SET RECOVERY FULL;

data.title: Restore from a full backup
data.code:
RESTORE DATABASE HR
FROM   DISK = 'D:\backup\hr.bak'
WITH   FILE = 1,
       REPLACE,

data.title: FILE = position
data.text: A single .bak file can contain multiple backups (appended with NOINIT). Use WITH FILE = N to restore the Nth backup. Always verify with RESTORE HEADERONLY first to see what is inside.
Security has two layers: *authentication* (who are you?) and *authorization* (what are you allowed to do?). SQL Server supports two authentication modes.

rows: Single sign-on, password policies enforced, more secure
Login name and password stored in SQL Server
Works for non-Windows clients, easier to manage remotely

data.title: Prefer Windows Authentication
data.text: Windows Authentication is more secure — passwords are never sent over the network, and it integrates with Active Directory policies. Use SQL Authentication only when Windows Auth is not possible (e.g., Linux clients, third-party applications).
Controlling access with GRANT, REVOKE, and DENY
Once authenticated, a user's access is controlled by permissions granted on *securables* (tables, views, etc.). Three statements manage the permission lifecycle:

rows: GRANT SELECT ON People TO peter
Remove a granted or denied permission
REVOKE SELECT ON People FROM peter
DENY INSERT ON People TO peter

data.title: Grant and deny permissions

data.text: Rather than granting permissions to individuals, use roles — named collections of permissions assigned to groups of users. SQL Server includes fixed server and database roles, and you can create custom ones.

data.title: Creating and using a custom role
Protection essentials
points: Full backups are the base of recovery; differentials capture changes since the last full; transaction log backups chain in between
Use the FULL recovery model for production databases that need point-in-time restore
Prefer Windows Authentication over SQL Authentication for better security
GRANT gives permissions, DENY blocks them (overrides grants), REVOKE removes them
Use roles — not individual grants — to manage permissions for groups of users
